title: A New Creation and the Ministry of Reconciliation
summary: Paul contrasts the earthly tent of the present body with the eternal building God has prepared, and speaks of groaning for that future while walking by faith, with the Spirit as a pledge. Because all must appear before Christ's judgment seat, and because Christ's love compels him, Paul lives no longer for himself. Anyone in Christ is a new creation; God has reconciled the world to himself through Christ and entrusted the apostles with the message of reconciliation, pleading with people to be reconciled to God.
story: Chapter 4 ended with eyes fixed on what is unseen and eternal. Chapter 5 continues that thought: the present body is wasting away, but God has something better in store. From there Paul moves to the reason for his whole ministry and to one of the richest summaries of the gospel in the New Testament. Verses 11-21 explain why Paul persuades people, why his critics misjudge him, and what the message he carries actually is. The chapter's appeal, "Be reconciled to God", leads straight into the urgent plea of 6:1-2.
historical:
Paul had faced death recently (1:8-10), and he writes as someone who has thought hard about dying before the Lord returns. In his earlier letters he often wrote as though he might live to see Christ's coming (1 Thessalonians 4:15; 1 Corinthians 15:51). Here he reckons seriously with the possibility of dying first and asks what happens then. Some scholars think his outlook shifted; others think he always held both possibilities open.

The Corinthians had their own questions about the body. Some of them had denied the resurrection of the dead (1 Corinthians 15:12), probably under the influence of Greek ideas that the body was a prison of the soul and that salvation meant escape from it. Paul's language here, of not wishing to be unclothed but clothed, answers that view. His hope is not a bodiless existence but a new, resurrection body, when "our mortality may be swallowed up by life" (verse 4).
cultural:
Paul was a tentmaker (Acts 18:3), and the image of the body as a tent, a temporary dwelling that is taken down, came naturally to him. Tents also recalled Israel's time in the wilderness and the tabernacle, God's portable dwelling before the temple. The contrast with "a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands" sets the temporary against the permanent.

Several of Paul's words come from public life. The arrabon of verse 5 was a commercial term for a deposit or first installment that guaranteed the rest of the payment. The bema of verse 10 was the raised platform where a magistrate sat to judge; Acts 18:12 uses the same word for the tribunal where Paul stood before the proconsul Gallio in Corinth, so the Corinthians knew exactly what it looked like. Ambassadors (verse 20) represented a ruler to a foreign people and spoke in his name, and the language of reconciliation was used in the Greek world for settling disputes between estranged parties, including nations and spouses (1 Corinthians 7:11). What was new was the idea that the offended party, God, takes the initiative to reconcile.
literary: The chapter falls into two parts. Verses 1-10 use a cluster of images, tent and building, clothing and nakedness, home and away, to describe the tension of living between present mortality and future resurrection. Verses 11-21 turn from hope to motive and message. The logic runs in steps: Christ's love compels us (verse 14), one died for all (verses 14-15), so we regard no one according to the flesh (verse 16), so anyone in Christ is a new creation (verse 17), and all this is God's work of reconciliation (verses 18-19), which makes the apostles ambassadors (verse 20). Verse 21 ends with a balanced sentence that many readers consider the heart of the gospel in a single line: Christ, who knew no sin, was made sin; in him we become the righteousness of God.

outline.t: The earthly tent and the heavenly dwelling
Walking by faith and the judgment seat of Christ
Compelled by Christ's love: one died for all
God reconciles the world and sends ambassadors

doctrines.note: Verses 14-15 and 21 are among Paul's clearest statements of Christ's death: "One died for all", and God "made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf". Most interpreters see substitution here, Christ taking the place of sinners. Some read "to be sin" as "to be a sin offering", since in the Hebrew Old Testament the same word can mean sin and sin offering; others take it as Christ bearing sin itself. On either reading his death is for others.

Reconciliation is God's initiative from first to last: "All this is from God". God does not wait for the world to make peace with him; he was reconciling the world to himself in Christ, not counting trespasses. Humans are called to receive it: "Be reconciled to God".

Believers too "must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ" (verse 10). This is not a second trial of their salvation but an accounting of how they have lived, a sober motive for faithful living set alongside the assurance of reconciliation.

Christian hope is embodied. Paul longs not to be unclothed but clothed with a heavenly dwelling, and he has the Spirit as the pledge. Between death and resurrection believers are "at home with the Lord" (verse 8), but the final hope is mortality swallowed up by life.

words.note: Katallasso, to reconcile, to change enmity into friendship. In Paul, God is always the one who reconciles and humans are the ones reconciled; God is never said to be reconciled to us. The word appears three times in verses 18-20 with its noun twice, making this the densest passage on reconciliation in the Bible.

Ktisis, creation. Verse 17 has no verb in the Greek, which reads, literally, if anyone in Christ, new creation. Interpreters debate whether Paul means the person is made new or that the person now belongs to God's new creation, the renewed world begun in Christ's resurrection. The two are connected, and both echo Isaiah's promise of new things (Isaiah 43:18-19; 65:17).

Arrabon, pledge, deposit, or first installment, a Semitic loanword used in Greek business. It guarantees the full payment to come. The Spirit is God's down payment on the resurrection life he has promised (also 1:22; Ephesians 1:14).

Presbeuo, to act as an ambassador. An ambassador speaks for another and carries his authority. Paul describes the apostles as God making "His appeal through us": the message is God's, not theirs, and so is its urgency.

christ: Here Christ is the one whose love compels, whose death is for all, and in whom God reconciles the world to himself. He "knew no sin", yet God made him to be sin on our behalf, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (verse 21). Interpreters describe that exchange in different ways. The Reformation tradition reads it as imputation, Christ's righteousness counted to believers as their sin was counted to him. Others, including N. T. Wright, read "the righteousness of God" here as God's covenant faithfulness embodied in the apostles' ministry. Both agree that Christ's death is the ground of reconciliation. He is also the judge before whom all will stand (verse 10), and his resurrection ("was raised again", verse 15) opens the new creation into which believers now enter.
questions: Paul says Christ died so that those who live should "no longer live for themselves". What would that look like in one specific area of your life this week?
Verse 16 says we no longer regard anyone according to the flesh. How does being a new creation change the way you see other people, not only yourself?
Reconciliation here begins with the offended party. What would it cost you to take the first step toward someone you are estranged from?
